title: AML Agents Briefing — Friday, 07 August 2026
script:
ALEX: Welcome to AML Agents Briefing. It's Thursday the seventh of August 2026, and this is your audio overview of today's most material APAC AML and financial crime developments. Full detail, the obligation register, and horizon scanning are all at amlagents dot streamlit dot app.

JORDAN: Big day, Alex. We've got SEBI enforcement completions out of India, a clutch of obligations worth flagging for Australia, Indonesia, and Hong Kong, and some important horizon items for digital currency exchanges and Tranche 2 readiness. Let's get into it.

ALEX: Starting with the top story. The Securities and Exchange Board of India has issued release orders and formally recorded the completion of two recovery certificates from 2021, both connected to the same enforcement matter involving CAT Technologies Ltd. Recovery Certificate 4397 was issued against Kesava Mallikarjuna Prasad Chivukula, and Recovery Certificate 4396 was issued against Dhaduvai Venkatram. Both are now closed.

JORDAN: Alex, what does a completed recovery certificate actually signal in practical terms? Is this just administrative closure?

ALEX: It's more than housekeeping. In SEBI's enforcement framework, a recovery certificate is issued when a monetary penalty or disgorgement order hasn't been voluntarily paid. Completion means the amount has been recovered, either through seizure, attachment, or payment. The release order then lifts any encumbrance on the individual's assets. So this is the end of a multi-year enforcement cycle that began with the original order back in 2021.

JORDAN: And the read-across for compliance teams across the region?

ALEX: The CAT Technologies matter involves a listed entity and named individuals. For financial institutions with Indian market exposure, that's a reminder to run periodic screening against SEBI's published enforcement list, not just at onboarding. Five years can pass between an original order and its completion. Your sanctions and adverse-media screening needs to catch both the open and the closed enforcement lifecycle.

JORDAN: Exactly right. If you're running correspondent banking or custody relationships touching Indian capital markets, pull your periodic review schedule this week and confirm that SEBI's enforcement database is a named source in your adverse-media vendor configuration. Don't assume it's covered by default.

ALEX: Moving on to obligations. There are three dates worth flagging for teams across the region, and while the deadlines themselves are technically past, they carry carry-forward risk if your institution hasn't already filed.

JORDAN: The first is AUSTRAC. Under Part 13 of the AUSTRAC AML/CTF Rules, the annual compliance report for the calendar year 2024 reporting period was due on the thirty-first of March 2025. Late lodgement attracts daily civil penalties, and a misleading attestation carries criminal liability under Section 137 of the relevant legislation. If your Australian reporting entity is in any doubt about whether that return was lodged correctly, escalate to your AUSTRAC relationship contact now, not at your next board cycle.

ALEX: The second is Indonesia. Under POJK 12 of 2017, the annual independent review of the AML and CFT programme covering calendar year 2024 was due to the Risk Oversight Committee and the Board of Commissioners by the thirtieth of June 2025. If you're the MLRO at an Indonesian bank or finance company and that review hasn't been presented to the Dewan Komisaris, that's a governance gap your next PPATK examination will surface.

JORDAN: And the third is Hong Kong. The HKMA's AML and CFT Guideline, at paragraph eleven, requires authorised institutions to submit an annual self-assessment return covering the 2024 reporting period by the thirtieth of September 2025. That's submitted via the HKMA's prescribed Excel template, with independent validation from Internal Audit. If you're a head of financial crime compliance at an authorised institution, verify that your Internal Audit sign-off is documented and that the submission confirmation is on file.

ALEX: Now let's turn to what's on the horizon. Jordan, you flagged some high-priority items from the scanning feeds.

JORDAN: Yes, and the one I'd lead with is the AUSTRAC enforcement action against a major digital currency exchange. AUSTRAC announced a forty-seven million Australian dollar civil penalty for systemic failures in transaction monitoring, mule-account detection, and suspicious matter report timeliness. This caps a twelve-month investigation.

ALEX: Forty-seven million is a significant number, and the fact that it covers three distinct failure categories is important. It's not one gap. It's a programme-wide breakdown.

JORDAN: Right, and the lesson for digital currency exchange compliance officers registered with AUSTRAC is straightforward. Pull your last quarter of SMR metrics, check your average time from detection to lodgement, and map your mule-account detection controls against the transaction velocity indicators that AUSTRAC has been publishing in its guidance. If you can't answer those questions before your next risk committee, that's a red flag.

ALEX: Also on the horizon, AUSTRAC has published detailed Tranche 2 industry guidance for legal practitioners, covering customer engagement triggers, source-of-wealth diligence in conveyancing, and legal professional privilege carve-outs. And separately, Bank Negara Malaysia has released a typology bulletin on investment scams routed through digital banks and crypto exchanges, with specific mule-account indicators including rapid post-onboarding velocity spikes.

JORDAN: For AML teams at digital banks and electronic money institutions in Malaysia, add those BNM mule-account indicators to your transaction monitoring rule review scope this month. The onboarding-to-velocity pattern is the specific signal BNM is calling out.

ALEX: So what are the two or three things listeners should do this week?

JORDAN: First, verify your SEBI adverse-media coverage is active and current, particularly if you have Indian capital markets exposure. Second, if you're AUSTRAC-registered as a digital currency exchange, run a self-assessment against the three failure categories in that penalty notice before your next board or risk committee. And third, for anyone in Malaysia, pull the BNM typology bulletin and sense-check your mule-detection logic against it.

ALEX: That's the briefing for today. Full detail, the obligation register, and source links are all waiting for you at amlagents dot streamlit dot app.

JORDAN: That's where you'll find the horizon calendar, the full digest, and everything you need to brief your team. See you tomorrow.
